subject: اللغة الإنجليزية
lesson: Grammar Recall: first conditional and first conditional with modals
outcomes: Form the first conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb
Use modals (may, might, could, should, can) in first conditional sentences
Talk about future jobs using conditional sentences

tf.s: The first conditional is formed with if + present simple, will + base verb.
tf.why: That is the basic pattern of the first conditional.

tf.s: The first conditional talks about real or possible situations in the future.
tf.why: It describes things that can really happen.

tf.s: 'If it will rain tomorrow, we stay at home' is correct.
tf.why: Use the present simple after if: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.'

tf.s: 'Might' and 'may' can replace 'will' to show possibility.
tf.why: They show the result is possible, not certain.

tf.s: 'Will' shows the result is less certain than 'might'.
tf.why: 'Will' is more certain; 'might' only shows possibility.

tf.s: 'Should' in the result clause can give advice.
tf.why: For example: If you feel tired, you should rest.

tf.s: The if clause can come first or second in the sentence.
tf.why: Both orders are correct; use a comma when the if clause comes first.

tf.s: In the first conditional, the result clause uses the past simple.
tf.why: The result clause uses will (or a modal) + base verb.

tf.s: 'If he doesn't work harder, he will lose his job' is a correct first conditional.
tf.why: If + present simple (negative), will + base verb.

tf.s: After a modal verb like 'can', we add -s to the verb: 'can goes'.
tf.why: Modals are followed by the base verb: 'can go'.

boxes.why: 'Might' means it is possible but not certain.

boxes.why: First conditional uses will in the result.

boxes.q: Is the first conditional about the past or the future?
boxes.why: It talks about possible future situations.

mcq.q: How do we form the first conditional?
o: If + present simple, will + base verb
If + past simple, would + base verb
mcq.why: This is the pattern for real future situations.

mcq.q: Which modal can replace 'will' to show possibility?
mcq.why: May and might show that something is possible.

mcq.q: What kind of situation does the first conditional describe?
o: A real or possible situation in the future
An imaginary situation in the past
A finished action in the past
A general rule that never changes
mcq.why: The first conditional is about real future possibilities.

mcq.q: Which form comes after a modal verb?
mcq.why: Modals are followed by the base form, e.g. 'might go'.

o: If you go to Canada, you'll have a great time.
If you will go to Canada, you have a great time.
If you went to Canada, you'll have a great time.
If you go to Canada, you having a great time.
mcq.why: If + present simple, will + base verb.

mcq.q: Your friend has a headache. Which first conditional gives advice?
o: If you have a headache, you should rest.
If you had a headache, you rested.
If you will have a headache, you rest.
If you have a headache, you might to rest.
mcq.why: Should + base verb gives advice in the result clause.

mcq.q: Complete about your future job: 'If I study hard, I ___ a chef.'
mcq.why: The result clause uses will + base verb.

mcq.q: What is the difference between 'If I pass, I will go to university' and 'If I pass, I might go to university'?
o: 'Will' is certain; 'might' shows it is only possible
There is no difference in meaning
If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
We will stay at home if it rains tomorrow.
If it rains tomorrow, we may stay at home.
mcq.why: Do not use 'will' in the if clause; use the present simple.

mcq.q: 'If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.' Is the situation real or imaginary, present or future?
mcq.why: It is a real possibility about tomorrow.
